''The Exponential Series.''—20. Denoting the complex number <math>x+iy</math> by <math>z</math>, let us consider the series <math>1+z+z^2/2!+\dots+z^n/n!+\dots</math> This series converges uniformly and absolutely for all values of <math>z</math> whose moduli do not exceed an arbitrarily chosen positive number <math>\text{R}</math>. Consequently the function <math>E(z)</math>, defined as the limiting sum of the above series, is continuous in every finite domain. The two series representing <math>E(z_1)</math> and <math>E(z_2)</math>, when multiplied together give the series represented by <math>E(z_1+z_2)</math>. In accordance with a known theorem, since the series for <math>E(z_1)</math> <math>E(z_2)</math> are absolutely convergent, we have <math>E(z_1)\times E(z_2)=E(z_1+z_2)</math>. From this fundamental relation, we deduce at once that <math>\{E(z)\}^n=E(nz)</math>, where <math>n</math> is any positive integer. The number <math>E(1)</math>, the sum of the convergent series <math>1+1+1/2!+1/3!\dots</math>, is usually denoted by <math>e</math>; its value can be shown to be <math>2{\cdot}718281828459\dots</math> It is known to be a transcendental number, ''i.e.'' it cannot be the root of any algebraical equation with rational coefficients; this was first established by Hermite. Writing <math>z=1</math>, we have <math>E(n)=e^n</math>, where <math>n</math> is a positive integer. If <math>z</math> has as a value a positive fraction <math>p/q</math>, we find that <math>\{E(p/q)\}^q=E(p)=e^p</math>; hence <math>\text{E}(p/q)</math> is the real positive value of <math>e^{p/q}</math>. Again <math>E(-p/q)\times E(p/q)=E(0)=1</math>, hence <math>E(-p/q)</math> is the real positive value of <math>e^{-p/q}</math>. It has been thus shown that for any real and rational number <math>x</math>, the value of <math>E(x)</math> is the principal value of <math>e^x</math>. This result can be extended to irrational values of <math>x</math>, if we assume that <math>e^x</math> is for such a value of <math>x</math> defined as the limit of the sequence <math>e^{x_1}, e^{x_2},\dots</math>, where <math>x_1, x_2,\dots</math> is a sequence of rational numbers of which <math>x</math> is the limit, since <math>E(x_1)</math>, <math>E(x_2)\dots</math>, then converges to <math>E(x)</math>.

Next consider <math>(1+z/m)^m</math>, where <math>m</math> is a positive integer. We have by the binomial theorem,
{{block center|<math>\left(1+\frac{z}{m}\right)^m=1+z+\left(1-\frac{1}{m}\right)\frac{z^2}{2!}+.+\left(1-\frac{1}{m}\right)\left(1-\frac{2}{m}\right)\dots</math>}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|278|TRIGONOMETRY|}}</noinclude><math>(a+\iota b)^{m/n}</math> are obtained by giving <math>s</math> the values <math>0, 1, 2, \dots n-1</math> in the expression <math>r^{m/n}\ (\cos\ m.\overline{\theta+2s\pi}/n + \iota \sin\ m.\overline{\theta+2s\pi}/n)</math>, where <math>r=(a^2+b^2)^{\frac{1}{2}}</math> and <math>\theta=\text{arc tan}\ b/a</math>. l representation of the complex <math>B_3,\dots B_n</math> represent the expression <math>x+\iota y</math>, <math>(x+\iota y)^2</math>, <math>(x+\iota y)^3</math>, <math>\dots (x+\iota y)^n</math> respectively, the triangles <math>OAB_1</math>, <math>OB_1B_2</math>, <math>\dots OB_{n-1}B_n</math> are all similar. Let <math>(x+\iota y)^n = a+\iota b</math>, then the converse problem of finding the <math>n</math>th root of <math>a+\iota b</math> is equivalent to the geometrical problem of describing such a series of triangles that <math>OA</math> is the first side of the first triangle and <math>OB_n</math> the second side of the <math>n</math>th. Now it is obvious that this geometrical problem has more solutions than one, since any number of complete revolutions round <math>O</math> may be made in travelling from <math>B_1</math> to <math>B_n</math>. The first solution is that in which the vertical angle of each triangle is <math>B_nOA/n</math>; the second is that in which each is <math>(B_nOA+2\pi)/n</math>, lution being made round <math>O</math>; the third has <math>(B_nOA+4\pi)/n</math> for the vertical angle of each triangle; and so on. There are <math>n</math> sets of triangles which satisfy the required conditions. For simplicity we will take the case of the determination of the values of <math>(\cos\theta + \iota \sin\theta)^{\frac{1}{3}}</math>. Suppose <math>B</math> to represent the expression <math>\cos\theta + \iota\sin\theta</math>. If the angle <math>AOP_1</math> is <math>\tfrac{1}{3}\theta</math>, <math>P_1</math> represent the root <math>\cos\tfrac{1}{3}\theta + \iota\sin\tfrac{1}{3}\theta</math>; the angle <math>AOB</math> is filled up by the angles of the three similar triangles <math>AOP_1</math>, <math>P_1Op_1</math>, <math>p_1OB</math>. Also, if <math>P_2</math>, <math>P_3</math> be such that the angles <math>P_1OP_2</math> <math>P_1OP_3</math> are <math>\tfrac{2}{3}\pi</math>, <math>\tfrac{4}{3}\pi</math> respectively, the two sets of triangles <math>AOP_2</math>, <math>P_2Op_3</math>, <math>p_3OB</math> and <math>AOP_3</math>, <math>P_3Op_2</math>, <math>p_2OB</math> satisfy the conditions of similarity and of having <math>OA</math>, <math>OB</math> for the bounding sides; thus <math>P_2</math>, <math>P_3</math> represent the roots sides; thus <math>\text{P}_2</math>, <math>\text{P}_3</math> represent the roots <math>\cos\tfrac{1}{3}(\theta+2\pi)+\iota\ \sin\ \tfrac{1}{3}(\theta+2\pi)</math>, <math>\cos\ \tfrac{1}{3}(\theta+4\pi)+\iota\ \sin\ \tfrac{1}{3}(\theta+4\pi)</math> respectively. If <math>B</math> coincides with <math>A</math>, the problem is reduced to that of finding the three cube roots of unity. One will be represented by <math>A</math> and the others by the two angular points of an equilateral triangle, with <math>A</math> as one angular point, inscribed in the circle.

'''''The <math>n</math>th Roots of Unity.''''' The problem of determining the values of the <math>n</math>th roots of unity is equivalent to the geometrical problem of inscribing a regular polygon of <math>n</math> sides in a circle. Gauss has shown in his ''Disquisitiones arithmeticae'' that this can always be done by the compass and ruler only when <math>n</math> is a prime of the form <math>2^p+1</math>. The determination of the <math>n</math>th root of any complex number requires in addition, for its geometrical solution, the division of an angle into <math>n</math> equal parts.

'''''Factorizations.''''' 19. We are now in a position to factorize an expression of the form <math>x^n-(a+\iota b)</math>. Using the values which we have obtained above for <math>(a+\iota b)^{1/n}</math>, we have
{{block center|<math>x^n-(a+\iota b) = \underset{s=0}{\overset{s=n-1}{P}} \left[x-r^{\frac{1}{n}}\left(\cos\frac{\theta+2s\pi}{n}+\iota\sin\frac{\theta+2s\pi}{n}\right)\right].</math> (1)}}
If <math>b=0</math>, <math>a=1</math>, this becomes
{{block center|<math>x^n-1 = \underset{s=0}{\overset{s=n-1}{P}} \left[x-\cos\frac{2s\pi}{n}-\iota\sin\frac{2s\pi}{n}\right]</math>}}
{{block center|<math>= (x-1)(x+1)\underset{s=1}{\overset{s=\frac{1}{2}n-1}{P}} \left(x-\cos\frac{2s\pi}{n}\pm\iota\sin\frac{2s\pi}{n}\right)</math>}}
{{block center|<math>= (x-1)(x+1)\underset{s=1}{\overset{s=\frac{1}{2}n-1}{P}} \left(x^2-2x\cos\frac{2s\pi}{n}+1\right)</math> (<math>n</math> even). (2) <math>x^n-1=(x-1)\mathop{\text{P}}_{s=1}^{s=\frac{1}{2}(n-1)}\left(x^2-2x\cos\frac{2s\pi}{n}+1\right)</math> (''n'' odd). (3)}}
If in (1) we put <math>a=-1</math>, <math>b=0</math>, and therefore <math>\theta=\pi</math>, we have
{{block center|<math>x^n+1=\mathop{\text{P}}_{s=0}^{s=n-1}\left[x-\cos\frac{\overline{2s+1\pi}}{n}-\iota\sin\frac{\overline{2s+1\pi}}{n}\right]</math>}}
{{block center|<math>=\mathop{\text{P}}_{s=0}^{s=\frac{1}{2}(n-2)}\left[x^2-2x\cos\frac{\overline{2s+1\pi}}{n}+1\right]</math> (''n'' even). (4)}}
{{block center|<math>x^n+1=(x+1)\mathop{\text{P}}_{s=0}^{s=\frac{1}{2}(n-3)}\left[x^2-2x\cos\frac{\overline{2s+1\pi}}{n}+1\right]</math> (''n'' odd). (5)}} Also <math>x^{2n}-2x^ny^n\cos n\theta+y^{2n}</math>

{{block center|<math>=(x^n-y^n\,\overline{\cos n\theta+\iota\sin n\theta})(x^n-y^n\,\overline{\cos n\theta-\iota\sin n\theta})</math>}}

{{block center|<math>=\overset{s=n-1}{\underset{s=0}{P}}\left(x-y\,\overline{\cos\frac{\theta+2s\pi}{n}\pm\iota\sin\frac{\theta+2s\pi}{n}}\right)</math>}}

{{block center|<math>=\overset{s=n-1}{\underset{s=0}{P}}\left[x^2-2xy\cos\theta+\frac{2s\pi}{n}+y^2\right].</math> (6)}}

Airy and Adams have given proofs of this theorem which do not involve the use of the symbol <math>\iota</math> (see ''Camb. Phil. Trans.'', vol. xi).

A large number of interesting theorems may be derived from De Moivre's theorem and the factorizations which we have deduced from it; we shall notice one of them.

''Example of De Moivre's Theorem.''—In equation (6) put <math>y=1/x</math>, take logarithms, and then differentiate each side with respect to <math>x</math>, and we get

{{block center|<math>\frac{2n(x^{2n-1}-x^{-2n-1})}{x^{2n}-2\cos n\theta+x^{-2n}}=\sum_{s=0}^{s=n-1}\frac{2(x-x^{-3})}{x^2-2\cos\theta+\frac{2s\pi}{n}+x^{-2}}.</math>}}

Put <math>x^2=a/b</math>, then we have the expression

{{block center|<math>\frac{n(a^{2n}-b^{2n})}{(a^2-b^2)(a^{2n}-2a^nb^n\cos n\theta+b^{2n})}</math>}}

for the sum of the series

{{block center|<math>\sum_{s=0}^{s=n-1}\frac{1}{a^2-2ab\cos\overline{\theta+\frac{2s\pi}{n}}+b^2}.</math>}}

''The Exponential Series.''—20. Denoting the complex number <math>x+iy</math> by <math>z</math>, let us consider the series <math>1+z+z^2/2!+\dots+z^n/n!+\dots</math> This series converges uniformly and absolutely for all values of <math>z</math> whose moduli do not exceed an arbitrarily chosen positive number <math>\text{R}</math>. Consequently the function <math>E(z)</math>, defined as the limiting sum of the above series, is continuous in every finite domain. The two series representing <math>E(z_1)</math> and <math>E(z_2)</math>, when multiplied together give the series represented by <math>E(z_1+z_2)</math>. In accordance with a known theorem, since the series for <math>E(z_1)</math> <math>E(z_2)</math> are absolutely convergent, we have <math>E(z_1)\times E(z_2)=E(z_1+z_2)</math>. From this fundamental relation, we deduce at once that <math>\{E(z)\}^n=E(nz)</math>, where <math>n</math> is any positive integer. The number <math>E(1)</math>, the sum of the convergent series <math>1+1+1/2!+1/3!\dots</math>, is usually denoted by <math>e</math>; its value can be shown to be <math>2{\cdot}718281828459\dots</math> It is known to be a transcendental number, ''i.e.'' it cannot be the root of any algebraical equation with rational coefficients; this was first established by Hermite. Writing <math>z=1</math>, we have <math>E(n)=e^n</math>, where <math>n</math> is a positive integer. If <math>z</math> has as a value a positive fraction <math>p/q</math>, we find that <math>\{E(p/q)\}^q=E(p)=e^p</math>; hence <math>\text{E}(p/q)</math> is the real positive value of <math>e^{p/q}</math>. Again <math>E(-p/q)\times E(p/q)=E(0)=1</math>, hence <math>E(-p/q)</math> is the real positive value of <math>e^{-p/q}</math>. It has been thus shown that for any real and rational number <math>x</math>, the value of <math>E(x)</math> is the principal value of <math>e^x</math>. This result can be extended to irrational values of <math>x</math>, if we assume that <math>e^x</math> is for such a value of <math>x</math> defined as the limit of the sequence <math>e^{x_1}, e^{x_2},\dots</math>, where <math>x_1, x_2,\dots</math> is a sequence of rational numbers of which <math>x</math> is the limit, since <math>E(x_1)</math>, <math>E(x_2)\dots</math>, then converges to <math>E(x)</math>.

Next consider <math>(1+z/m)^m</math>, where <math>m</math> is a positive integer. We have by the binomial theorem,
{{block center|<math>\left(1+\frac{z}{m}\right)^m=1+z+\left(1-\frac{1}{m}\right)\frac{z^2}{2!}+.+\left(1-\frac{1}{m}\right)\left(1-\frac{2}{m}\right)\dots \left(1-\frac{s-1}{m}\right)\frac{z^s}{s!}+\dots+\left(\frac{z}{m}\right)^m.</math>}}
Also
{{block center|<math>\left(1-\frac{1}{m}\right)\left(1-\frac{2}{m}\right)\dots\left(1-\frac{s-1}{m}\right)</math>}}
lies between <math>1</math> and
{{block center|<math>1+\left(\frac{1}{m}+\frac{2}{m}+\dots+\frac{s-1}{m}\right);</math>}}
hence the product equals <math>1-\theta_s s\,.\,s-1/2m</math> where <math>\theta_s</math> is such that <math>0<\theta_s<1</math>.

We have now
{{block center|<math>\left(1+\frac{z}{m}\right)^m=1+z+\left(1-\frac{1}{m}\right)\frac{z^2}{2!}+\dots+\left[1-\theta_s\frac{s\,.\,s-1}{2m}\right]\frac{z_s}{s!}+\dots</math>}}
{{block center|<math>+\left[1-\theta_m\frac{m-1}{2}\right]\frac{z^m}{m!}</math>}}
{{block center|<math>=1+z+z^2/2!+\dots+z^s/s!+\text{R}_s,</math>}}
where
{{block center|<math>\text{R}_s=\frac{z^{s+1}}{(s+1)!}+\dots+\frac{z^m}{m!}-\frac{z^2}{2m}\biggl\{1+\theta_3\frac{2}{1}+\dots</math>}}
{{block center|<math>+\theta_s\frac{z^{s-2}}{(s-2)!}+\dots+\theta_m\frac{z^{m-2}}{(m-2)!}\biggr\}.</math>}}
Since the series for <math>E(z)</math> converges, <math>s</math> can be fixed so that for all values of <math>m>s</math> the modulus of <math>z^{s+1}/(s+1)!+\dots+z^m/m!</math> is less than an arbitrarily chosen number <math>\tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon</math>. Also the modulus of <math>1+\theta_3z/1+\dots+\theta_m z^{m-2}/(m-2)!</math> is less than that of <math>1+1\,|z|/1!+|z|^2/2!+\dots</math>, or of <math>e^{\text{mod}\,z}</math>, hence <math>\text{mod}\ \text{R}_s<\tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon+(1/2m)</math>. <math>\text{mod}\ (z^2e^z)<\epsilon</math>, if <math>m</math> be chosen sufficiently great. It follows that <math>\lim_{m=\infty}(1+z/m)^m=E(z)</math>, where <math>z</math> is any complex number.
